EXCLUSIVE FULL-SHIP CHARTER · SPRING 2027

SouthGeorgia

FALKLANDS · SOUTH GEORGIA · PUNTA ARENAS TO PUNTA ARENAS · 17 DAYS · 16 NIGHTS · MAGELLAN EXPLORER · PC·SG/27

South Georgia in early spring, when few ships go: snow to the waterline, king penguin colonies of hundreds of thousands, and elephant seal bulls fighting for their harems as pups are born every day. We charter the whole of Magellan Explorer, so the timing follows wildlife, weather and light, with three days in the Falklands, six on South Georgia and only 88 guests with 16 guides, led by Phototeva’s wildlife photographers.

At a glance

The short answers

What is this expedition?

A 17-day, 16-night voyage from Punta Arenas, Chile, to the Falkland Islands and South Georgia aboard the 88-guest Magellan Explorer, chartered in full for two departures in September and October 2027 and built around wildlife photography.

Why early spring?

October brings the elephant seal breeding season, huge king penguin colonies with eggs and chicks, snow-covered scenery and low-angle light, with fewer aggressive male fur seals on the beaches, so more landings stay open.

What will I see?

King, gentoo, rockhopper, macaroni and Magellanic penguins, elephant and fur seals, black-browed and wandering albatross, giant petrels, Shackleton’s grave at Grytviken and the glaciers of Drygalski Fjord. Sightings are never guaranteed.

How active is it?

Moderate. Twice-daily Zodiac landings with walks on snow, shingle and tussock; an optional 6 km hike on Shackleton’s route. Boots are lent on board; the guides help with every Zodiac step.

The route

Punta Arenas · Saunders · Carcass · Stanley · Elsehul · Salisbury Plain · Fortuna · Stromness · Grytviken · St Andrews · Ocean Harbour · Gold Harbour · Drygalski · Bleaker · New Island

DAY 01 / 17 · SUN 26 SEP 2027PC·SG · D01

Embark in Punta Arenas

Board Magellan Explorer on the Punta Arenas waterfront, meet the Phototeva guides and sail east through the Strait of Magellan as the Patagonian light fades.

Transfer from your hotel to the pier in the afternoon and board Magellan Explorer, the 88-guest polar ship chartered in full for this departure. Cabins, safety drill and a welcome from the expedition team and Phototeva's photographers, then the ship slips east past the two narrows of the Strait of Magellan with Commerson's dolphins often riding the bow. Dinner as Patagonia falls astern.

At sea · bound for the Falklands

A full day crossing the Patagonian shelf: albatross and petrels astern, mandatory IAATO and biosecurity briefings, and the first photography workshops.

DAY 03 / 17 · TUE 28 SEP 2027PC·SG · D03

Saunders & Carcass · five penguins in a day

The Neck on Saunders Island, where gentoo, rockhopper, Magellanic and king penguins share a sandy isthmus beside a black-browed albatross colony; then rat-free Carcass Island and tea at the settlement.

Saunders Island's Neck is one of the richest wildlife sites in the South Atlantic: gentoos on the beach, rockhoppers bouncing up the cliffs, Magellanic penguins braying from burrows, a few king penguins and black-browed albatross nesting on the slopes. In the afternoon Carcass Island, free of rats and cats, is loud with Cobb's wrens and tussock birds; walk the shore past Magellanic penguins to the settlement for tea and cakes before the overnight run along the north coast to Stanley.

DAY 04 / 17 · WED 29 SEP 2027PC·SG · D04

Stanley, Falkland Islands

A morning in Stanley, the small capital: the whalebone arch at Christ Church Cathedral, the Historic Dockyard Museum and old wrecks in the harbour, before the ship turns east for South Georgia.

Magellan Explorer anchors off Stanley and Zodiacs run guests ashore. Walk the waterfront to Christ Church Cathedral and its arch of blue-whale jawbones, visit the Historic Dockyard Museum for the islands' maritime and Antarctic history, and look for the hulks of nineteenth-century sailing ships in the harbour. Post a card, find a pint at a harbour pub, and be back aboard after lunch for the 800-nautical-mile run to South Georgia.

  • Stanley · Port William51°40.32′S 057°43.80′W

DAY 05 / 17 · THU 30 SEP 2027PC·SG · D05

Scotia Sea · towards South Georgia

The ship crosses the Antarctic Convergence into colder, bird-rich water. Lectures on Shackleton, South Georgia's wildlife and composition in snow, and the first icebergs on the radar.

Somewhere today the sea temperature drops by several degrees as the ship crosses the Antarctic Convergence, and the birdlife changes with it: wandering and grey-headed albatross, diving petrels, prions in flocks. Inside, the programme runs from Shackleton's 1916 crossing of South Georgia to post-processing workshops. Watch the radar for the first icebergs.

DAY 06 / 17 · FRI 1 OCT 2027PC·SG · D06

Shag Rocks & the last sea miles

A second sea day past the Shag Rocks pinnacles, with whales and icebergs increasingly likely, gear checks for the landings and a full biosecurity inspection.

South Georgia's strict biosecurity rules mean every bag, pocket and Velcro strip is checked and vacuumed today. Between inspections, watch for humpback and fin whales feeding near Shag Rocks and for the first tabular icebergs drifting north from the Weddell Sea. The guides finish the landing briefings, and by evening the island's snow peaks may rise on the eastern horizon.

DAY 07 / 17 · SAT 2 OCT 2027PC·SG · D07

Elsehul & Salisbury Plain

A Zodiac cruise in sheltered Elsehul, among fur seals, macaroni penguins and nesting albatross, then the vast king penguin colony on Salisbury Plain below the Grace Glacier.

At the island's north-western tip, Elsehul is a narrow bay walled with tussock where fur seals lie on the snow and macaroni penguins nest in the cliffs; in early spring there are fewer male fur seals, so the Zodiac cruise can work close to shore. In the afternoon, Salisbury Plain in the Bay of Isles holds one of the largest king penguin colonies on Earth: a moving carpet of adults, eggs and brown woolly chicks stretching up the glacial outwash plain, with elephant seals hauled out along the beach.

DAY 08 / 17 · SUN 3 OCT 2027PC·SG · D08

Fortuna Bay & Shackleton's last mile

Land in Fortuna Bay among king penguins and elephant seals, then follow the final section of Shackleton's 1916 crossing over the saddle to the whaling station at Stromness, snow permitting.

Fortuna Bay has a king penguin colony at the foot of the König Glacier and elephant seal harems on the beach. Conditions allowing, guests then hike the last stage of Shackleton, Worsley and Crean's 1916 crossing, about 6 km over a snow saddle and down the waterfall to Stromness, while the ship repositions to meet them. The old whaling station, where the three men walked in after 36 hours, is closed for safety but the beach and valley are full of seals.

  • Fortuna Bay54°07.80′S 036°48.00′W
  • Stromness54°09.30′S 036°42.00′W

DAY 09 / 17 · MON 4 OCT 2027PC·SG · D09

Grytviken · Shackleton's grave

A full day at Grytviken: the restored whaling station, the South Georgia Museum, the Norwegian church of 1913, and a toast at the graves of Ernest Shackleton and Frank Wild.

Grytviken was the first whaling station on South Georgia, founded in 1904. Walk among the rusting boilers and the beached Petrel, visit the South Georgia Museum and the white Norwegian church, and gather at the little cemetery where Sir Ernest Shackleton was buried in 1922, with his right-hand man Frank Wild beside him. The government officers at King Edward Point clear the ship in, and there is time to photograph elephant seal pups among the ruins.

  • Grytviken54°16.68′S 036°29.70′W

DAY 10 / 17 · TUE 5 OCT 2027PC·SG · D10

St Andrews Bay & Ocean Harbour

South Georgia's largest king penguin colony, hundreds of thousands strong below three glaciers, then the wreck of the Bayard in Ocean Harbour.

St Andrews Bay is the island's largest king penguin colony, a crowd of birds packed between the Cook, Buxton and Heaney glaciers, with elephant seal harems along the black-sand beach and bulls fighting in the surf. The early landing catches low spring light on the colony. In the afternoon, Ocean Harbour holds the hulk of the Bayard, a three-masted ship wrecked here in 1911, and a small whalers' graveyard among the tussock.

  • St Andrews Bay54°26.10′S 036°09.90′W

DAY 11 / 17 · WED 6 OCT 2027PC·SG · D11

Gold Harbour · battle season

Gold Harbour at dawn: the Bertrab Glacier hanging above a beach of king penguins and elephant seal harems, where bulls of up to four tonnes defend their cows and new pups arrive daily.

Early October is the height of the elephant seal breeding season. At Gold Harbour, dominant bulls weighing up to four tonnes hold harems of cows on the beach and see off challengers in roaring, bloody fights, while newborn pups suckle among them. King penguins stand along the tideline and gentoos nest above. The sun rises behind the Bertrab Glacier, so the first Zodiac goes in at dawn; the rest of the day is for a longer landing or a Zodiac cruise under the ice cliffs.

  • Gold Harbour54°36.90′S 035°55.80′W

DAY 12 / 17 · THU 7 OCT 2027PC·SG · D12

Drygalski Fjord · ice and farewell

Ship cruise into Drygalski Fjord, a narrow cleft at the south-east end of the island ending at the Risting Glacier, with snow petrels against the ice; then the ship turns west.

Drygalski Fjord cuts some 14 km into the mountains at the island's south-eastern end, its walls streaked with hanging glaciers and its head blocked by the Risting Glacier. The ship noses in as far as the ice allows while snow petrels, pure white, wheel along the cliffs. Ice and weather permitting there may be a last Zodiac cruise at Larsen Harbour, before Magellan Explorer heads west for the Falklands.

  • Drygalski Fjord54°48.00′S 036°04.80′W

DAY 15 / 17 · SUN 10 OCT 2027PC·SG · D15

Bleaker & New Island

Rockhopper penguins and a busy imperial shag colony on Bleaker Island in the south, then the albatross and rockhopper cliffs of New Island at the far west of the archipelago.

Bleaker Island is low and green, with rockhopper and gentoo penguins and one of the larger imperial shag colonies in the Falklands; the morning landing walks the coast among them. The ship then runs west along the south of the islands to New Island, a nature reserve where black-browed albatross, rockhopper penguins and imperial shags nest together on the western cliffs, a last landing in long evening light.

Life aboard

Magellan Explorer · polar capability, boutique comfort

The vessel

Chartered in full

Magellan Explorer

A purpose-built polar expedition ship launched in 2019, with advanced stabilisers for a smoother crossing and a cruising speed of up to 14 knots to maximise time in the field. Spacious cabins and suites, many with private balconies, panoramic lounges, a restaurant, library, gym and sauna. For these departures the whole ship is chartered: 88 guests, 16 guides.

Launched2019

Travel information

Before you go
Getting there

Fly to Punta Arenas (PUQ) in southern Chile, usually via Santiago (SCL), about three and a half hours. Arrive the day before boarding; on day 17 the ship is alongside around midday, so book onward flights for mid-afternoon or later.

Your guides

The photography programme is led by Phototeva: founder Roie Galitz, a wildlife photographer with over 50 polar expeditions and more than 150 international awards, and Yarin Klein, a wildlife photographer and expedition guide with more than a decade leading trips in the High Arctic, the sub-Antarctic islands and Africa.

Weather in spring

Expect −3 to +5 °C, snow showers, sunny spells and strong winds that can change quickly. Long days with sunrise around 06:00 and sunset after 19:30 in October give long golden hours for photography.

What to wear and bring

Layers: thermal base, fleece and a waterproof, windproof outer shell with waterproof trousers, warm hat, gloves you can shoot in, and sunglasses. Boots are lent on board. Bring two camera bodies if you have them, a 100–400 mm or longer lens, a wide angle and a dry bag.

Biosecurity

South Georgia has some of the strictest biosecurity in the world. Every item that goes ashore is inspected and vacuumed, boots are disinfected before and after every landing, and you keep at least 5 m from wildlife.

Health & fitness

You need to step in and out of Zodiacs with help and walk on snow, shingle and tussock. The Shackleton hike is optional. There is a doctor on board; travel insurance must include medical evacuation.

Questions travellers ask

FAQ
When is the best time to visit South Georgia?

Early spring (late September to October) brings elephant seal harems and fights, king penguin colonies with eggs and chicks, snow-covered scenery and fewer male fur seals, so more landing sites stay open. Midsummer has greener slopes and more fur seals.

How long does it take to sail from the Falklands to South Georgia?

About two and a half days. Stanley to South Georgia is roughly 800 nautical miles; at Magellan Explorer’s cruising speed of up to 14 knots the crossing takes two full sea days.

What does a full-ship charter mean for guests?

The whole ship is booked for this group, so the itinerary, landing times and pace are set around wildlife, weather and photography rather than a standard cruise schedule. It also means only 88 guests with 16 guides.

Can I visit Shackleton’s grave?

Yes. Grytviken, where Sir Ernest Shackleton was buried in 1922 beside Frank Wild, is a full-day stop with the South Georgia Museum and the whalers’ church of 1913.

Do I need to be a photographer to join?

No. The voyage is photography-focused, with Phototeva’s guides running workshops and image reviews, but wildlife lovers who just want to be there are equally welcome.

How much does the South Georgia spring expedition cost?

From US$14,795 per person in a Porthole Cabin to US$19,995 in a Penthouse Suite, for 17 days and 16 nights full board, on departures from 26 September and 12 October 2027.
